source.text: Ἀδελφοί, ἡ μὲν εὐδοκία τῆς ἐμῆς καρδίας καὶ ἡ δέησις πρὸς τὸν θεὸν ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν εἰς σωτηρίαν.

records.literal_gloss: Brothers, the indeed desire of the my heart and the prayer to the God on behalf of them [is] for salvation.

en.L: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, the desire of my heart and [my] prayer to God for them [is] for [their] salvation.
en.B: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, what my heart longs for, and what I ask God for them, is that they may be saved.
en.R: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, I long with all my heart for my people Israel to be saved. That is what I pray to God for them.

decisions.choice: desire, what the heart longs for
decisions.reason: εὐδοκία can mean God's good pleasure or a person's goodwill, but beside "of my heart" and "prayer" it is Paul's own deep wish.

decisions.choice: "them" is the people of Israel who have not believed
alternatives: the Jews in general, believers included
decisions.reason: The pronoun looks back to Israel in 9:31-33, which pursued the law but stumbled over the stone. Paul's grief for them began in 9:1-3.

decisions.choice: the "on the one hand" has no matching "on the other"
decisions.reason: μὲν usually expects a contrasting clause with "but". None follows; the contrast is implied in verses 2-3, where Paul turns to what is wrong.

decisions.choice: my people Israel
decisions.reason: Readable names who "them" are (meaning note m2), since a new reader may start here.

source.text: μαρτυρῶ γὰρ αὐτοῖς ὅτι ζῆλον θεοῦ ἔχουσιν· ἀλλ’ οὐ κατ’ ἐπίγνωσιν, ἀγνοοῦντες γὰρ τὴν τοῦ θεοῦ δικαιοσύνην, καὶ τὴν ἰδίαν ζητοῦντες στῆσαι, τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ τοῦ θεοῦ οὐχ ὑπετάγησαν·

records.literal_gloss: I bear witness for to them that zeal of God they have; but not according to knowledge, \v 3 being ignorant of for the of the God righteousness, and the own seeking to establish, to the righteousness of the God not they submitted;

en.L: For I testify about them that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. \v 3 For being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish [their] own, they did not submit to the righteousness of God.
en.B: I can vouch for them that they are eager for God, but their eagerness is not guided by real understanding. \v 3 They did not recognize the righteousness of God, and in trying to set up a righteousness of their own, they would not submit to the righteousness that comes from God.
en.R: I can tell you that they are very eager to serve God. But they do not really understand. \v 3 They did not know about the righteousness of God: how God puts people right with {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}. They tried to have a righteousness of their own instead. So they would not accept the righteousness God gives.

decisions.choice: zeal for God: eager devotion to God
decisions.reason: ζῆλος is burning eagerness. Paul knew it from the inside: he had been zealous for the traditions of his fathers and had persecuted the church (Galatians 1:13-14, Philippians 3:6).

decisions.choice: knowledge that rightly understands
decisions.reason: ἐπίγνωσις is knowledge that recognizes the truth (as in 1:28). Israel did not lack information; what was missing was a right understanding of what God was doing, which verse 3 explains.

decisions.choice: the righteousness of God: God's own way of putting people right with himself, which he gives
alternatives: God's own justice as a quality of God
decisions.reason: As in 1:17 and 3:21-22, God's righteousness is God acting to put people right, received by faith. It stands against "their own", a righteousness of their own based on the law, as Paul says of himself in Philippians 3:9.

decisions.choice: they did not submit themselves
decisions.reason: ὑπετάγησαν is passive in form but has the sense of submitting oneself, as often with this verb. Not submitting means refusing to accept God's way and trusting their own instead.

decisions.choice: eager to serve God; how God puts people right with himself; the righteousness God gives
decisions.reason: Readable explains "zeal for God" and "the righteousness of God" as meaning notes m1 and m3 describe, as Romans 1:17 does at Readable. Reviewers should check that the explanation does not narrow the phrase.

decisions.choice: the righteousness that comes from God
decisions.reason: Balanced varies the repeated phrase in the second half of verse 3 so that the long sentence reads naturally; it keeps the sense of meaning note m3.

source.text: τέλος γὰρ νόμου Χριστὸς εἰς δικαιοσύνην παντὶ τῷ πιστεύοντι.

records.literal_gloss: End for of law [is] Christ unto righteousness to everyone the believing.

en.L: For {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} [is the] end of [the] law for righteousness to everyone who believes.
en.B: For {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} is the end of the law, bringing righteousness to everyone who believes.
en.R: {{christos:Christ|The Messiah}} is the end of the law. Through {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, everyone who believes can be righteous before God.

decisions.choice: end: the law has come to its end as the way to righteousness
alternatives: goal: the law was always pointing to Christ
both: the law reaches its goal in Christ and so its end
decisions.reason: τέλος can mean an end, a goal, or an outcome. The contrast in verses 3-6 between a righteousness of one's own from the law and the righteousness from faith favors "end": in Christ the law is no longer the way to be right with God. But Paul has just said that Israel pursued the law and did not reach it (9:31), and he says the law itself bears witness to God's righteousness (3:21, 3:31), which favors "goal". A word for "end" that also allows "goal" keeps both readings open.

decisions.choice: the result: righteousness for everyone who believes
alternatives: a limit on "end": Christ ends the law as a means to righteousness
decisions.reason: The phrase "for righteousness" may say what Christ brings (righteousness for every believer), or in what respect the law has ended (as a way to righteousness). Both readings say that righteousness now comes to everyone who believes; the levels follow the first.

decisions.choice: the law: the law of Moses
decisions.reason: There is no article, but the law in view is the law Israel pursued (9:31) and that Moses wrote (verse 5).

decisions.choice: Through him ... can be righteous before God
decisions.reason: Readable makes the short phrase into a clause and says who brings it; "before God" says where righteousness counts.

source.text: Μωϋσῆς γὰρ γράφει ὅτι τὴν δικαιοσύνην τὴν ἐκ τοῦ νόμου ὁ ποιήσας ἄνθρωπος ζήσεται ἐν αὐτῇ.

records.literal_gloss: Moses for writes that the righteousness the from the law: the [one] having done [it] man will live by it.

en.L: For Moses writes [about] the righteousness that [is] from the law, that the {{gender:person|man}} who has done [it] will live by it.
en.B: Moses writes this about the righteousness that comes from the law: "The {{gender:person|man}} who does it will live by it."
en.R: Moses writes about the righteousness that comes from keeping the law. He says, "The {{gender:person|man}} who does what the law commands will live by doing it."

decisions.choice: Leviticus 18:5
decisions.reason: In Leviticus 18:5 God tells Israel to keep his statutes and rules, for the person who does them will live by them. Paul quotes the same verse in Galatians 3:12. Here he uses it to describe the way of righteousness based on doing.

decisions.choice: "will live by it" (by the righteousness)
alternatives: "will live by them" (by the commandments), with the word order changed, as in Leviticus
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT has "by it", referring to the righteousness. Many manuscripts have "them", the reading of Leviticus 18:5, and place "that" differently. The meaning is close either way. Reviewers must check the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the principle of law-righteousness: life depends on doing
alternatives: a promise Paul rejects as false
decisions.reason: Paul does not deny what Leviticus says. He sets it beside the righteousness from faith (verse 6): righteousness from the law depends on doing what it commands, and no one is put right with God that way (3:20).

decisions.choice: from keeping the law; what the law commands; by doing it
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what "from the law" and "does it" mean.

source.text: ἡ δὲ ἐκ πίστεως δικαιοσύνη οὕτως λέγει· Μὴ εἴπῃς ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ σου· Τίς ἀναβήσεται εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν; τοῦτ’ ἔστιν Χριστὸν καταγαγεῖν·

records.literal_gloss: The but from faith righteousness thus speaks: Not you should say in the heart of you: Who will ascend into the heaven? That is, Christ to bring down;

en.L: But the righteousness [that is] from faith speaks thus: "Do not say in your heart, 'Who will ascend into heaven?'" (that is, to bring {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} down);
en.B: But the righteousness that comes from faith speaks like this: "Do not say in your heart, 'Who will go up into heaven?'" (that is, to bring {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} down).
en.R: But the righteousness that comes by faith speaks in a different way. It says, "Do not say to yourself, 'Who will go up to heaven?'" Asking that would mean someone has to go up and bring {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} down.

decisions.choice: the question and Paul's comment on it are one record
alternatives: "that is, to bring Christ down" as a sentence on its own, as the SBLGNT's question mark allows
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT ends the quoted question with a question mark, but the next words, τοῦτ ἔστιν ("that is"), are Paul's comment on that question and cannot stand alone. The record keeps them together; the meaning is the same either way.

decisions.choice: Deuteronomy 30:12, with "Do not say in your heart" from Deuteronomy 9:4
decisions.reason: In Deuteronomy 30:11-14 Moses tells Israel that God's command is not too hard or far away: it is not in heaven, so that someone must go up and fetch it, nor beyond the sea, but very near. "Do not say in your heart" comes from Deuteronomy 9:4, a warning against thinking that Israel earned the land by its own righteousness. Paul lets the righteousness from faith speak in Moses' words.

decisions.choice: the righteousness from faith speaks, as if a person
decisions.reason: Paul sets two voices side by side: Moses writing about law-righteousness (verse 5) and the righteousness from faith speaking for itself. The word "but" marks the contrast.

decisions.choice: say in your heart: think to yourself
decisions.reason: In the Old Testament, to say something in one's heart is to think it privately (Psalm 14:1).

decisions.choice: as if Christ had not already come down from heaven
alternatives: as if a person had to climb to heaven to find righteousness
decisions.reason: Paul's comment, "that is", applies the question to Christ. To ask who will go up to heaven would be to act as though Christ still had to be brought down, when he has already come. Righteousness does not have to be fetched; God has brought it near.

decisions.choice: Asking that would mean someone has to go up and bring the Messiah down
alternatives: that is, to bring Christ down
decisions.reason: Readable spells out what Paul's short comment means (meaning note m5).

decisions.choice: speaks in a different way
decisions.reason: Readable makes the contrast with verse 5 explicit.

source.text: ἤ· Τίς καταβήσεται εἰς τὴν ἄβυσσον; τοῦτ’ ἔστιν Χριστὸν ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναγαγεῖν.

records.literal_gloss: Or: Who will descend into the abyss? That is, Christ out of dead to bring up.

en.L: or, "Who will descend into the abyss?" (that is, to bring {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} up from [the] dead).
en.B: Or, "Who will go down into the abyss?" (that is, to bring {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} back up from the dead).
en.R: Or, "Who will go down into the deep, to the place of the dead?" Asking that would mean someone has to go down and bring {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} back from the dead.

decisions.choice: the question and Paul's comment on it are one record
alternatives: "that is, to bring Christ up from the dead" as a sentence on its own
decisions.reason: As in verse 6, the SBLGNT ends the question with a question mark, but Paul's comment that follows cannot stand alone.

decisions.choice: Deuteronomy 30:13, reworded
alternatives: a new saying of Paul's own
decisions.reason: Deuteronomy 30:13 asks who will cross the sea to bring the command back. Paul has "go down into the abyss" instead. In the Old Testament the deep of the sea and the depths below the earth are pictures of death, from which God brings his people up again (Psalm 71:20, Jonah 2:2-6), so the change fits Paul's point about Christ rising from the dead.

decisions.choice: the abyss: the depths, the place of the dead
decisions.reason: ἄβυσσος is the deep, used in the Greek Old Testament for the depths of the sea and of the earth. Paul's comment, "to bring Christ up from the dead", shows that he means the place of the dead.

decisions.choice: as if Christ had not already been raised
decisions.reason: To ask who will go down to the dead would be to act as though Christ had not already been raised by God. Both his coming and his rising are done; nothing is left for people to do to bring him near.

decisions.choice: to the place of the dead; Asking that would mean someone has to go down
decisions.reason: Readable explains "the abyss" (meaning note m3) and spells out Paul's comment as in verse 6.

source.text: ἀλλὰ τί λέγει;

records.literal_gloss: But what says it?

en.L: But what does it say?
en.B: But what does it say?
en.R: So what does it say?

decisions.choice: "it" is the righteousness from faith (verse 6), speaking in the words of Scripture
decisions.reason: The subject is not named. It continues the voice of verse 6, which speaks in the words of Deuteronomy 30, so it is the righteousness from faith speaking through Scripture.

source.text: Ἐγγύς σου τὸ ῥῆμά ἐστιν, ἐν τῷ στόματί σου καὶ ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ σου, τοῦτ’ ἔστιν τὸ ῥῆμα τῆς πίστεως ὃ κηρύσσομεν.

records.literal_gloss: Near you the word is, in the mouth of you and in the heart of you; that is the word of the faith which we proclaim.

en.L: "Near you is the word, in your mouth and in your heart"; that is, the word of faith which we proclaim.
en.B: "The word is close to you, on your lips and in your heart." This is the message of faith that we proclaim.
en.R: It says, "The message is close to you. It is on your lips and in your heart." This is the message about faith that we preach.

decisions.choice: Deuteronomy 30:14
decisions.reason: Moses says the word is very near, in your mouth and in your heart, "so that you can do it". Paul leaves out the last words and applies the verse to the message about Christ.

decisions.choice: word: the spoken message
decisions.reason: ῥῆμα is a spoken word or message. Here it is the gospel message Paul and others proclaim.

decisions.choice: the word of faith: the message that calls for faith and is received by faith
alternatives: the message that is the faith, the content of what Christians believe
decisions.reason: The genitive "of faith" ties the message to faith: it is about believing and it is received by believing, as verses 9-10 explain.

decisions.choice: in the mouth and in the heart: something one can say and believe
decisions.reason: Mouth and heart stand for speaking and inner conviction. Verses 9-10 take up the two words: confessing with the mouth and believing in the heart.

decisions.choice: message
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "message" for what is proclaimed, since "word" in English usually means one word. Balanced keeps "word" in the quotation.

decisions.choice: on your lips
decisions.reason: "On your lips" is how English speaks of words a person says.

decisions.choice: It says
decisions.reason: Readable repeats who is speaking, since the question is in a separate sentence.

source.text: ὅτι ἐὰν ὁμολογήσῃς ἐν τῷ στόματί σου κύριον Ἰησοῦν, καὶ πιστεύσῃς ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ σου ὅτι ὁ θεὸς αὐτὸν ἤγειρεν ἐκ νεκρῶν, σωθήσῃ·

records.literal_gloss: That if you confess with the mouth of you Lord Jesus, and you believe in the heart of you that the God him raised out of dead, you will be saved;

en.L: That if you confess with your mouth Jesus [as] Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} from [the] dead, you will be saved;
en.B: If you declare with your lips that Jesus is Lord, and in your heart believe that God raised {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} from the dead, then you will be saved.
en.R: If you say out loud, "Jesus is Lord," and you believe deep inside that God raised {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} from death, you will be saved.

decisions.choice: "that": this is what the message of faith says
alternatives: "because": the reason the word is near
decisions.reason: ὅτι may give the content of the message just mentioned or the reason it is near. The content fits best: this is the word of faith Paul proclaims. Either way the promise is the same.

decisions.choice: confess: declare openly
decisions.reason: ὁμολογέω is to say the same thing, to agree and declare publicly. Here it is an open statement of who Jesus is, not a confession of sin.

decisions.choice: "Jesus is Lord": an early Christian confession
decisions.reason: The words are a short statement of faith (1 Corinthians 12:3, Philippians 2:11). In the Greek Old Testament "Lord" stands for the divine name, and verse 13 applies a verse about the Lord to Jesus.

decisions.choice: mouth and heart: the whole person, speaking and trusting
alternatives: two separate steps that must be done in order
decisions.reason: Paul takes the two words from Deuteronomy 30:14 (verse 8). Speaking and believing go together; verse 10 gives them in the reverse order.

decisions.choice: declare with your lips (B); say out loud (R)
decisions.reason: "Confess" in English often means admitting wrong (meaning note m2); Balanced and Readable say "declare" and "say out loud".

decisions.choice: deep inside
decisions.reason: Readable says what "in your heart" means.

source.text: καρδίᾳ γὰρ πιστεύεται εἰς δικαιοσύνην, στόματι δὲ ὁμολογεῖται εἰς σωτηρίαν·

records.literal_gloss: With heart for it is believed unto righteousness, with mouth and it is confessed unto salvation;

en.L: For with [the] heart it is believed for righteousness, and with [the] mouth it is confessed for salvation;
en.B: For people believe with the heart, and this leads to righteousness; they confess with the mouth, and this leads to salvation.
en.R: People believe with their heart, and God counts them righteous. They say with their mouth what they believe, and God saves them.

decisions.choice: a general statement about anyone who believes
decisions.reason: Both verbs are impersonal passives, "it is believed", "it is confessed": they state what happens for every believer, not for a particular person.

decisions.choice: two parallel lines that say one thing
alternatives: righteousness and salvation as two stages, one by believing and one by confessing
decisions.reason: Paul repeats verse 9 in the reverse order and in balanced lines. Righteousness and salvation are not separate gifts for separate acts; the lines together describe one response of faith and its result.

decisions.choice: leading to, resulting in
decisions.reason: εἰς gives the result: believing ends in righteousness, confessing ends in salvation.

decisions.choice: God counts them righteous; God saves them
decisions.reason: Readable makes God the one who gives righteousness and salvation, as 4:3-5 says that God counts faith as righteousness. Reviewers should check that this does not say more than the verse.

source.text: λέγει γὰρ ἡ γραφή· Πᾶς ὁ πιστεύων ἐπ’ αὐτῷ οὐ καταισχυνθήσεται.

records.literal_gloss: Says for the Scripture: Everyone the believing on him not will be put to shame.

en.L: For the Scripture says, "Everyone who believes on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} will not be put to shame."
en.B: For the Scripture says, "Whoever believes in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} will not be put to shame."
en.R: Scripture says, "No one who believes in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} will ever be let down or left in shame."

decisions.choice: Isaiah 28:16, quoted already in 9:33
decisions.reason: Isaiah speaks of a stone God lays in Zion: the one who believes will not be put to shame. The Hebrew has "will not be in haste" (will not panic); Paul follows the Greek translation. Here he adds "everyone", which leads into verses 12-13.

decisions.choice: "him" is Christ, the stone of 9:33
decisions.reason: In 9:33 the stone is Christ, over whom Israel stumbled, and verse 9 has just spoken of believing about Jesus. So "him" is Christ.

decisions.choice: not be put to shame: not be disappointed or disgraced
decisions.reason: To be put to shame is to have one's trust prove empty, especially at God's judgment. Those who believe in him will find their trust was not misplaced.

decisions.choice: will ever be let down or left in shame
alternatives: will not be put to shame
decisions.reason: Readable explains the idiom (meaning note m3).

source.text: οὐ γάρ ἐστιν διαστολὴ Ἰουδαίου τε καὶ Ἕλληνος, ὁ γὰρ αὐτὸς κύριος πάντων, πλουτῶν εἰς πάντας τοὺς ἐπικαλουμένους αὐτόν·

records.literal_gloss: Not for is difference of Jew both and of Greek, the for same Lord of all, being rich toward all the [ones] calling on him;

en.L: For there is no distinction of Jew and Greek, for the same [one is] Lord of all, being rich toward all who call on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}};
en.B: Here there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, for one and the same Lord is Lord over everyone, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} gives generously to all who call on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.
en.R: In this, Jews and people who are not Jews are no different. The same Lord rules over all of them. He gives richly to everyone who calls out to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} for help.

decisions.choice: Greek: anyone who is not a Jew
decisions.reason: Paired with "Jew", "Greek" stands for all non-Jews, as in 1:16 and 2:9-10.

decisions.choice: the Lord is Jesus
decisions.reason: Verse 9 has just named Jesus as Lord, and verse 13 speaks of calling on the name of the Lord. The Lord of all is the same Lord. Paul said in 3:29-30 that God is God of Jews and Gentiles alike; here the same is said of the Lord Jesus.

decisions.choice: rich toward: generous, giving richly
decisions.reason: πλουτέω is to be rich; with "toward all" it means pouring out riches on them, as Paul speaks of the riches of God's kindness (2:4).

decisions.choice: call on: pray to, appeal to for help
decisions.reason: To call on someone is to cry out to him in prayer and trust. Verse 13 takes the phrase from Joel.

decisions.choice: gives generously (B); gives richly (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable turn the picture into what the rich Lord does.

decisions.choice: calls out to him for help
decisions.reason: Readable explains "call on" (meaning note m4).

decisions.choice: people who are not Jews
decisions.reason: Readable says what "Greek" means here, as in 1:16.

source.text: Πᾶς γὰρ ὃς ἂν ἐπικαλέσηται τὸ ὄνομα κυρίου σωθήσεται.

records.literal_gloss: Everyone for who ever calls on the name of Lord will be saved.

en.L: For "everyone who calls on the name of [the] Lord will be saved."
en.B: For "all who call on the name of the Lord will be saved."
en.R: As Scripture says, "Everyone who calls out to the Lord for help will be saved."

decisions.choice: Joel 2:32 (3:5 in the Hebrew)
decisions.reason: Joel promises that in the day of the Lord everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. Paul quotes the Greek translation exactly, without a formula. In the Hebrew, "the Lord" is the divine name, YHWH.

decisions.choice: the Lord called on is Jesus
decisions.reason: In Joel the Lord is Israel's God. Paul has just said "Jesus is Lord" (verse 9) and "the same Lord" (verse 12), and in verse 14 people must believe in the one they call on. So Paul applies Joel's words to Jesus.

decisions.choice: call on the name: pray to and trust in the Lord
decisions.reason: In the Old Testament, the name stands for the person; to call on the Lord's name is to pray to him and rely on him (Genesis 4:26, Psalm 116:4).

decisions.choice: As Scripture says; calls out to the Lord for help
alternatives: For; calls on the name of the Lord
decisions.reason: Readable says that this is a quotation and explains the idiom (meaning note m3).

source.text: Πῶς οὖν ἐπικαλέσωνται εἰς ὃν οὐκ ἐπίστευσαν;

records.literal_gloss: How then may they call on [him] in whom not they believed?

en.L: How then may they call on [the one] in whom they have not believed?
en.B: How, then, are they to call on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} if they have not believed in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}?
en.R: But how can people call out to the Lord if they have not believed in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}?

decisions.choice: a chain of questions: each step needs the one before
decisions.reason: Verses 14-15 run backward from calling on the Lord to believing, hearing, preaching and being sent. Each "how" question expects the answer that it cannot happen without the step before. The verbs are deliberative: how could they?

decisions.choice: "they": people in general, with Israel in view
decisions.reason: The questions state what must be true for anyone to call on the Lord (verse 13: "everyone"). From verse 16 Paul applies them to Israel, who heard but did not obey.

decisions.choice: him (B); the Lord (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the one called on, the Lord of verse 13.

source.text: πῶς δὲ πιστεύσωσιν οὗ οὐκ ἤκουσαν;

records.literal_gloss: How and may they believe [him] whom not they heard?

en.L: And how may they believe [in the one] whom they have not heard?
en.B: And how are they to believe in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} if they have never heard {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}?
en.R: And how can they believe in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} if they have never heard {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}?

decisions.choice: whom they have not heard: Christ heard speaking in the message
alternatives: of whom they have not heard: they have not heard about him
decisions.reason: οὗ with the verb "hear" most naturally means hearing a person, not hearing about him. Paul may mean that Christ himself is heard when his messengers speak (verse 17, "the word of Christ"). Many read it as "about whom", and the point is close either way.

source.text: πῶς δὲ ἀκούσωσιν χωρὶς κηρύσσοντος;

records.literal_gloss: How and may they hear without [one] preaching?

en.L: And how may they hear without [someone] preaching?
en.B: And how are they to hear without someone proclaiming?
en.R: And how can they hear unless someone tells them?

decisions.choice: preach: proclaim as a herald
decisions.reason: κηρύσσω is what a herald does: announce a message publicly on someone else's behalf. It leads into "sent" in verse 15.

source.text: πῶς δὲ κηρύξωσιν ἐὰν μὴ ἀποσταλῶσιν;

records.literal_gloss: How and may they preach if not they are sent?

en.L: And how may they preach unless they are sent?
en.B: And how are people to proclaim it unless they are sent?
en.R: And how can people go and tell them if no one sends them?

decisions.choice: sent as messengers
decisions.reason: ἀποστέλλω is to send someone on a mission with authority, the verb behind the word "apostle". Paul calls himself one sent in this way (1:1, 1:5).

decisions.choice: sent by God
decisions.reason: The verb is passive and does not say who sends. In Paul's letters it is God, through Christ, who sends messengers (1:1, Galatians 1:1); the readings agree that messengers must be sent before people can hear.

source.text: καθὼς γέγραπται· Ὡς ὡραῖοι οἱ πόδες τῶν εὐαγγελιζομένων τὰ ἀγαθά.

records.literal_gloss: Just as it has been written: How beautiful the feet of the [ones] bringing good news [of] the good [things].

en.L: Just as it is written, "How beautiful [are] the feet of those who bring good news of good things!"
en.B: As it is written, "How lovely are the feet of those who bring the good news of good things!"
en.R: As Scripture says, "How wonderful it is to see messengers coming with good news!"

decisions.choice: Isaiah 52:7
alternatives: Nahum 1:15, which has a similar line
decisions.reason: Isaiah pictures a runner arriving on the mountains with news for Jerusalem: peace, salvation, and "Your God reigns." Paul quotes it in a shorter form, closer to the Hebrew than to the Greek translation.

decisions.choice: beautiful feet: the welcome arrival of a messenger
decisions.reason: The feet are those of a runner bringing news. What makes them beautiful is the good news they carry.

decisions.choice: beautiful, lovely
alternatives: timely, coming at the right moment
decisions.reason: ὡραῖος can mean beautiful or ripe and timely. Both fit a messenger, but "beautiful" is the usual sense and the sense of the Hebrew.

decisions.choice: the shorter text
alternatives: many later manuscripts add "of those who bring good news of peace" before "of those who bring good news of good things"
decisions.reason: The earliest manuscripts have only the shorter line, and the SBLGNT follows them. The longer text fills in the line from Isaiah 52:7. Reviewers must check the apparatus.

decisions.choice: How wonderful it is to see messengers coming
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture (meaning note m2).

decisions.choice: lovely
decisions.reason: Balanced uses "lovely" for a welcome sight; Literal keeps "beautiful".

decisions.choice: Just as it is written (L); As it is written (B); As Scripture says (R)
alternatives: just as it has been written
decisions.reason: The formula for quoting Scripture, as in 1:17.

source.text: ἀλλ’ οὐ πάντες ὑπήκουσαν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ· Ἠσαΐας γὰρ λέγει· Κύριε, τίς ἐπίστευσεν τῇ ἀκοῇ ἡμῶν;

records.literal_gloss: But not all obeyed the gospel; Isaiah for says: Lord, who believed the report of us?

en.L: But not all obeyed the gospel; for Isaiah says, "Lord, who has believed our report?"
en.B: But not all have obeyed the gospel. Isaiah asks, "Lord, who has believed what we have told?"
en.R: But not everyone has accepted the good news and obeyed it. Isaiah says, "Lord, who has believed the message we told them?"

decisions.choice: obey: respond to the gospel with faith
decisions.reason: ὑπακούω is to listen and obey. For Paul, obeying the gospel is believing it, as the next words show and as 1:5 speaks of "the obedience of faith".

decisions.choice: Isaiah 53:1
decisions.reason: The words open Isaiah's song of the suffering servant. Paul quotes the Greek translation, which begins with "Lord"; the Hebrew has no word for "Lord" here.

decisions.choice: report: what was heard, the message
decisions.reason: ἀκοή means hearing or what is heard. In the quotation it is the message the prophet's people heard. Paul uses the same word in verse 17 for the hearing that faith comes from.

decisions.choice: "not all": an understatement for many
decisions.reason: Paul means that many in Israel did not obey, as the quotation and verses 18-21 show.

decisions.choice: accepted the good news and obeyed it
decisions.reason: Readable shows that obeying the gospel means accepting it (meaning note m1).

decisions.choice: what we have told (B); the message we told them (R)
decisions.reason: "Report" sounds like a document in modern English; Balanced and Readable say what was heard.

source.text: ἄρα ἡ πίστις ἐξ ἀκοῆς, ἡ δὲ ἀκοὴ διὰ ῥήματος Χριστοῦ.

records.literal_gloss: So the faith [is] from hearing, the and hearing through word of Christ.

en.L: So faith [is] from hearing, and hearing through [the] word of {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.
en.B: So faith comes from hearing the message, and the message is heard through the word about {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.
en.R: So faith comes from hearing the message. And the message people hear is the word about {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

decisions.choice: the word about Christ, the message that tells about him
alternatives: Christ's own word, Christ speaking through his messengers
Christ's command that sends the messengers
decisions.reason: Χριστοῦ may say whose word it is or what it is about. The message about Christ fits verses 8-9 best; the other readings fit verse 14 (hearing Christ) and verse 15 (being sent).

decisions.choice: hearing: the message heard
decisions.reason: ἀκοή is the same word as "report" in verse 16. Faith comes from hearing the message, and the message comes through the word about Christ.

decisions.choice: "of Christ"
decisions.reason: The earliest manuscripts have "of Christ", and the SBLGNT follows them. "Of God" is the more familiar phrase and may have replaced it. Reviewers must check the apparatus.

decisions.choice: a summary of verses 14-16
decisions.reason: ἄρα draws the conclusion: believing depends on hearing, and hearing depends on the message being spoken.

decisions.choice: comes from hearing the message; the message is heard
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable supply the verb and say what is heard.

source.text: Ἀλλὰ λέγω, μὴ οὐκ ἤκουσαν;

records.literal_gloss: But I say, not not did they hear?

en.L: But I say, [is it that] they did not hear?
en.B: But I ask, is it possible that they did not hear?
en.R: But I ask, is it true that they never heard the message?

decisions.choice: a question expecting the answer no: they did hear
decisions.reason: The Greek begins the question with μὴ, which expects a negative answer: surely it is not that they did not hear? Paul answers at once that they did.

decisions.choice: "they": Israel
decisions.reason: The next question names Israel (verse 19), and verse 16 has said that not all of Israel obeyed. Paul is asking whether Israel has an excuse.

decisions.choice: the message
decisions.reason: Readable says what was heard.

source.text: μενοῦνγε· Εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν ἐξῆλθεν ὁ φθόγγος αὐτῶν, καὶ εἰς τὰ πέρατα τῆς οἰκουμένης τὰ ῥήματα αὐτῶν.

records.literal_gloss: Rather indeed: Into all the earth went out the voice of them, and to the ends of the world the words of them.

en.L: On the contrary: "Into all the earth their voice went out, and to the ends of the world their words."
en.B: Indeed they did: "Their voice went out to the whole earth, and their words to the farthest parts of the world."
en.R: Yes, they did. As Scripture says, "Their voice has gone out into the whole earth. Their words have reached the ends of the world."

decisions.choice: an emphatic yes: indeed they did
decisions.reason: μενοῦνγε corrects or strengthens what was said before. After a question expecting "no", it confirms strongly that they did hear.

decisions.choice: Psalm 19:4 (18:5 in the Greek translation)
decisions.reason: Paul quotes the Greek translation word for word, without a formula. In the psalm the voice is that of the heavens, which declare God's glory to the whole earth. Paul uses the words for the message of the gospel messengers, which has gone out far and wide. The Hebrew has "their line" or "measuring line" where the Greek has "their voice".

decisions.choice: the message has spread widely: Israel has no excuse of not hearing
alternatives: every single person on earth had heard
decisions.reason: Paul uses the psalm's words to say that the gospel had already gone far beyond Judea, as he says of the faith of the Romans (1:8) and as Colossians 1:6 and 1:23 say. The point is that Israel cannot claim not to have heard.

decisions.choice: Yes, they did. As Scripture says
decisions.reason: Readable answers the question plainly and says that the words come from Scripture.

decisions.choice: On the contrary (L); Indeed they did (B)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the corrective particle; Balanced gives its force as an answer.

source.text: ἀλλὰ λέγω, μὴ Ἰσραὴλ οὐκ ἔγνω;

records.literal_gloss: But I say, not Israel not did know?

en.L: But I say, [is it that] Israel did not know?
en.B: Again I ask, is it possible that Israel did not understand?
en.R: And I ask, is it true that Israel did not understand?

decisions.choice: a question expecting the answer no: Israel did know
decisions.reason: As in verse 18, the question begins with μὴ and expects "no". Israel did know.

decisions.choice: what Israel knew: that the message would go to the nations and that Israel would refuse it
decisions.reason: The verb has no object. The quotations that follow, from Moses and Isaiah, say that God would make himself known to other nations and that Israel would resist. So Israel had been told in its own Scriptures what is now happening.

decisions.choice: understand
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "understand", since the question is whether Israel grasped the message, not whether it had heard it.

source.text: πρῶτος Μωϋσῆς λέγει· Ἐγὼ παραζηλώσω ὑμᾶς ἐπ’ οὐκ ἔθνει, ἐπ’ ἔθνει ἀσυνέτῳ παροργιῶ ὑμᾶς.

records.literal_gloss: First Moses says: I will provoke to jealousy you by not a nation, by a nation without understanding I will anger you.

en.L: First Moses says, "I will make you jealous by [those who are] not a nation; by a nation without understanding I will make you angry."
en.B: First, Moses says, "I will stir you to jealousy through those who are not a nation, and through a nation without understanding I will provoke your anger."
en.R: Moses was the first to speak about it. He wrote down what God said: "I will make you jealous of people who are not even a nation. I will make you angry with a nation that does not understand."

decisions.choice: Deuteronomy 32:21, in the Song of Moses
decisions.reason: In the song, Israel made God jealous with "no-gods", so God will make Israel jealous with a "no-people". Paul follows the Greek translation, changing "them" to "you" so that God addresses Israel directly.

decisions.choice: first: the first in a line of witnesses
alternatives: first in time, before anyone else
decisions.reason: Moses is the first witness Paul calls; Isaiah follows in verses 20-21.

decisions.choice: "not a nation": the Gentiles, who were not God's people
decisions.reason: Those who were not a nation in God's eyes are the Gentiles, now called God's people (9:25-26, quoting Hosea). Seeing them welcomed will stir Israel to jealousy, which Paul hopes will bring some to salvation (11:11, 11:14).

decisions.choice: make jealous: stir to jealousy
alternatives: make envious in a bad sense only
decisions.reason: παραζηλόω is to provoke jealousy. Paul returns to it in 11:11 and 11:14, where the jealousy is meant to bring Israel back.

decisions.choice: He wrote down what God said
decisions.reason: Readable says that the "I" of the quotation is God, speaking in Moses' song.

source.text: Ἠσαΐας δὲ ἀποτολμᾷ καὶ λέγει· Εὑρέθην ἐν τοῖς ἐμὲ μὴ ζητοῦσιν, ἐμφανὴς ἐγενόμην τοῖς ἐμὲ μὴ ἐπερωτῶσιν.

records.literal_gloss: Isaiah and is very bold and says: I was found by those me not seeking, manifest I became to those me not asking.

en.L: And Isaiah is very bold and says, "I was found by those not seeking {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}; I became visible to those not asking for {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."
en.B: Then Isaiah dares to say, "I was found by people who were not looking for {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}; I showed {{deity_pronoun:myself|Myself}} to those who never asked for {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."
en.R: Then Isaiah speaks even more boldly. He tells what God said: "People who were not looking for {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} have found {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. I showed {{deity_pronoun:myself|Myself}} to people who did not even ask about {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."

decisions.choice: Isaiah 65:1
decisions.reason: God speaks: he let himself be found by a people that did not call on his name. Paul quotes the Greek translation, with the two lines in the reverse order. Paul applies the words to the Gentiles; in verse 21 he applies the next verse to Israel.

decisions.choice: speaks boldly, dares
decisions.reason: ἀποτολμάω is to be very bold. Isaiah says something daring: that God was found by those who were not looking for him.

decisions.choice: those not seeking God: the Gentiles
alternatives: rebellious Israel, as some read Isaiah 65:1
decisions.reason: In 9:30 Paul has said that Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness obtained it. He reads Isaiah 65:1 the same way, and turns to Israel in verse 21.

decisions.choice: He tells what God said
decisions.reason: Readable says that the "I" of the quotation is God.

source.text: πρὸς δὲ τὸν Ἰσραὴλ λέγει· Ὅλην τὴν ἡμέραν ἐξεπέτασα τὰς χεῖράς μου πρὸς λαὸν ἀπειθοῦντα καὶ ἀντιλέγοντα.

records.literal_gloss: To but the Israel he says: All the day I stretched out the hands of me to a people disobeying and contradicting.

en.L: But about Israel he says, "All the day I stretched out {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} hands to a people disobeying and contradicting."
en.B: But about Israel he says, "All day long I have stretched out {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} hands to a people who disobey and argue back."
en.R: But about Israel, Isaiah tells what God said: "All day long I have held out {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} arms to welcome a people who would not obey {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} and kept arguing with {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}."

decisions.choice: Isaiah 65:2
decisions.reason: The verse follows the one quoted in verse 20. The Hebrew has "a rebellious people"; the Greek translation, which Paul quotes, has "a disobedient and contradicting people".

decisions.choice: about Israel
decisions.reason: πρὸς with Israel can mean "to" or "with reference to". The words are spoken about Israel, in contrast with the Gentiles of verse 20.

decisions.choice: "he" is Isaiah, still the speaker
decisions.reason: The subject continues from verse 20, where Isaiah is named. The "I" inside the quotation is God.

decisions.choice: stretched-out hands: a gesture of appeal and welcome
decisions.reason: Hands held out are a sign of pleading and of welcome. God has kept inviting Israel all day long, so the chapter ends with God's patience, not with his rejection of Israel (11:1).

decisions.choice: Isaiah tells what God said; to welcome
decisions.reason: Readable names Isaiah and God, and states the meaning of the gesture (meaning note m4).

decisions.choice: argue back (B); kept arguing with me (R)
decisions.reason: ἀντιλέγω is to speak against; Balanced and Readable use everyday words.
